title: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System
subtitle: Where along nucleus, fascicle, cistern, cavernous sinus, orbit, gaze center or pupillary pathway an eye-movement or pupil sign localizes

coreAnatomy.title: Ocular motor nuclei and crossing fibers

points.text: The superior rectus (CN III) and superior oblique (CN IV) are supplied by the contralateral nucleus; all other CN III muscles and the lateral rectus are supplied ipsilaterally.
points.quote: The superior rectus (CN III) and the superior oblique (CN IV) are innervated by neurons located on the contralateral side.

points.text: Because superior rectus fibers cross within the nuclear complex, a destructive lesion on one side denervates both superior recti.
points.quote: a destructive lesion in one superior rectus subnucleus results in bilateral denervation of the superior recti.

points.text: The levator has a single midline caudal subnucleus, so a nuclear CN III lesion gives bilateral ptosis.
points.quote: oculomotor nuclear lesions cause bilateral ptosis because the nuclear group for the levator of the lid is located in the midline

points.text: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is the unpaired, dorsal, rostral visceral column of the oculomotor complex and mediates pupillary constriction.
points.quote: contains the visceral nuclei (Edinger-Westphal nucleus) rostrally and the subnucleus for the LP superioris caudally

points.text: In the midbrain, the fascicles pass through the red nucleus before leaving the anterior midbrain medial to the cerebral peduncle; this explains Claude, Weber and Benedikt associations.
points.quote: diverge widely as they traverse the red nucleus before exiting on the anterior aspect of the midbrain just medial to the cerebral peduncles

points.text: In the subarachnoid space the nerve runs between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries and close to the uncus.
points.quote: each third nerve passes between the superior cerebellar and the posterior cerebral arteries, courses forward near the medial aspect of the uncus

points.text: In the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus CN III sits above CN IV and CN VI and medial to V1.
points.quote: the nerve runs over the trochlear nerve, lying superior to the abducens nerve, and medial to the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve

points.text: At the superior orbital fissure CN III splits into superior and inferior divisions; the book notes this split may exist more proximally, even in the fascicle.
points.quote: the oculomotor nerve divides into a superior division, which supplies the superior rectus and the LP superioris, and an inferior division

points.text: The trochlear fascicles decussate in the anterior medullary velum, so the nucleus supplies the opposite superior oblique.
points.quote: The nerve fascicles course posteroinferiorly around the aqueduct to decussate in the dorsal midbrain in the anterior medullary velum

points.text: The abducens nucleus lies in the dorsal lower pons next to the facial colliculus region.
points.quote: The paired abducens nucleus is located in the dorsal lower portion of the pons, separated from the floor of the fourth ventricle

points.text: Abducens interneurons project to the opposite MLF, which is why a nuclear lesion causes a gaze palsy and not only a lateral rectus palsy.
points.quote: The abducens motoneurons are intermixed with internuclear neurons that send their axons across the midline to the opposite MLF

points.text: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers travel briefly with the abducens nerve in the cavernous sinus.
points.quote: The third-order postganglionic neuron travels with the carotid artery into the cavernous sinus, onto the abducens nerve for a short course

points.text: The riMLF controls vertical and torsional saccades; a unilateral lesion slows downward saccades.
points.quote: Unilateral lesions of the riMLF cause slowing of downward saccades.

points.text: riMLF output to depressors is ipsilateral, while output to elevators is probably bilateral, which explains asymmetric vertical gaze palsies.
points.quote: projections to motoneurons innervating depressors (inferior rectus and superior oblique) are ipsilateral, whereas those innervating elevators

points.text: The INC is the integrator for upward gaze; its lesions affect vertical and torsional gaze holding rather than saccade speed.
points.quote: Unilateral lesions of the INC (the neural integrator for upward gaze) cause impaired vertical and torsional gaze holding.

points.text: A PPRF lesion abolishes ipsilateral saccades and quick phases while vestibular response, pursuit and gaze holding are preserved (dissociated gaze palsy).
points.quote: the PPRF is involved (dissociated ipsilateral horizontal conjugate gaze palsy)

points.text: Pupillary dilation uses an ipsilateral three-neuron sympathetic chain starting in the posterolateral hypothalamus and descending through the lateral brainstem tegmentum.
points.quote: Sympathetic innervation, which dilates the pupil, proceeds ipsilaterally from the posterolateral hypothalamus through the lateral tegmentum of the brainstem

points.text: Parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run with CN III and lie superficially in the nerve, which is why compression affects the pupil early.
points.quote: The pupillomotor fibers probably course in the periphery of the oculomotor nerve, immediately internal to the epineurium

localizationRules.explanation: A nuclear lesion gives an ipsilateral CN III palsy plus bilateral superior rectus weakness and bilateral incomplete ptosis; the pure unilateral nuclear lesion is very rare.
localizationRules.quote: More characteristic of nuclear involvement is unilateral third nerve palsy, weakness of the ipsilateral and contralateral superior rectus, and bilateral incomplete ptosis

localizationRules.rule: Pupil in peripheral CN III palsy
localizationRules.explanation: Ischemic lesions typically spare the pupil, whereas aneurysmal compression characteristically dilates and fixes it; the book notes exceptions in both directions.
localizationRules.quote: With ischemic lesions, the pupil is spared because the lesion is confined to the core of the nerve and spares peripherally situated pupillomotor fibers.

localizationRules.explanation: A third nerve palsy with Horner syndrome points to the cavernous sinus, and a sixth nerve palsy with ipsilateral Horner syndrome is likewise of localizing value there.
localizationRules.quote: Combined oculomotor paresis and sympathetic denervation are virtually pathognomonic of a cavernous sinus lesion.

localizationRules.rule: Trochlear nucleus or fascicle before decussation gives a contralateral palsy
localizationRules.explanation: In the midbrain the superior oblique palsy is contralateral to the lesion if the nucleus or pre-decussation fascicle is hit; outside the brainstem (subarachnoid space) it is usually ipsilateral.
localizationRules.quote: A lesion involving the trochlear nucleus or its fascicles before its decussation may result in contralateral paresis of the superior oblique muscle

localizationRules.rule: Abducens nucleus lesion equals ipsilateral gaze palsy
localizationRules.explanation: Do not call it a simple CN VI palsy: with a nuclear lesion both eyes fail to look to that side. A facial palsy often accompanies it.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions affecting the abducens nucleus cause not only an ipsilateral lateral rectus paresis but also an ipsilateral gaze palsy to the same side

localizationRules.explanation: Frontal gaze palsy can be overcome with the oculocephalic maneuver or calorics and is often transient; a pontine gaze palsy usually cannot be overcome and is long-lasting.
localizationRules.quote: Unilateral restriction of voluntary gaze to one side is most often due to contralateral frontal or ipsilateral pontine damage.

localizationRules.rule: Direction of skew deviation and tilt shows the level
localizationRules.explanation: Roll-plane tilt effects are ipsiversive with pontomedullary lesions below the crossing and contraversive with pontomesencephalic lesions at or above the MLF/INC level.
localizationRules.quote: All tilt effects in unilateral pontomesencephalic brainstem lesions are contraversive (contralateral eye lowermost) and indicate involvement of the MLF

localizationRules.rule: Downbeat nystagmus points to the craniocervical junction or cerebellum
localizationRules.explanation: Think cervicomedullary junction, midline medulla, or the posterior midline or diffuse cerebellum; the vestibulocerebellum (flocculus, nodulus, uvula) is most often responsible.
localizationRules.quote: DBN may occur with cervicomedullary junction disease, midline medullary lesions, posterior midline cerebellar lesions, or diffuse cerebellar disease

keySyndromes.name: Third nerve nuclear lesion
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral complete CN III palsy + contralateral ptosis + contralateral superior rectus paresis
keySyndromes.clue: The crossing superior rectus fibers and the single levator subnucleus make the findings bilateral for those two structures; the pupil is involved only with dorsal, rostral damage.
keySyndromes.quote: Ipsilateral complete CN III palsy; contralateral ptosis and superior rectus paresis

keySyndromes.name: Midbrain fascicular syndromes (Claude, Weber, Benedikt)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia and tremor (Claude, SCP/red nucleus) or contralateral hemiparesis (Weber, cerebral peduncle) or contralateral choreiform movements (Benedikt, red nucleus/substantia nigra)
keySyndromes.clue: The associated contralateral sign tells which structure beside the fascicle is involved.
keySyndromes.quote: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber)

keySyndromes.name: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Impaired upgaze + large pupils with light-near dissociation + convergence-retraction nystagmus and eyelid retraction (Collier sign)
keySyndromes.clue: Posterior commissure and rostral midbrain; ventral extension to the caudal central nucleus adds bilateral ptosis. Hydrocephalus and tumors are common causes.
keySyndromes.quote: The pupils are large and react poorly to light, but the near-response is spared (light-near dissociation).

keySyndromes.name: Pontine tegmental syndromes (Foville and Millard-Gubler)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + ipsilateral CN VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (Millard-Gubler)
keySyndromes.clue: Millard-Gubler is anterior paramedian and spares the abducens nucleus; Foville is the low dorsolateral pontine lesion with ipsilateral gaze palsy, facial paresis and dysmetria, plus contralateral hemiparesis if more extensive.
keySyndromes.quote: More anterior paramedian lesions spare the abducens nucleus but affect the fascicles, resulting in ipsilateral abducens and facial weakness with contralateral hemiparesis (Millard-Gubler syndrome).

keySyndromes.name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF syndrome)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral adduction weakness (adduction lag) + monocular nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye + convergence usually spared
keySyndromes.clue: Skew deviation often with the higher eye on the side of the lesion; bilateral INO with exotropia is WEBINO; a midbrain lesion high enough may impair convergence.
keySyndromes.quote: this syndrome is characterized by adduction weakness on the side of the MLF lesion and monocular nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye

keySyndromes.name: One-and-a-half syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Conjugate gaze palsy to one side + impaired adduction on looking to the other side + vertical movements and convergence spared
keySyndromes.clue: The lesion involves the PPRF or abducens nucleus plus the adjacent MLF on the side of the complete gaze palsy; exotropia of the eye opposite the lesion is common. Facial palsy gives the eight-and-a-half syndrome.
keySyndromes.quote: the only horizontal movement remaining is abduction of one eye, which exhibits nystagmus in abduction

keySyndromes.name: Gradenigo syndrome (petrous apex)
keySyndromes.triad: Abducens nerve paresis + ipsilateral facial (usually retroorbital) pain + deafness
keySyndromes.clue: Dorello canal and petrous tip; trigeminal involvement is more likely there than in the subarachnoid space, and otic discharge may point to the petrous bone.
keySyndromes.quote: Gradenigo syndrome, which includes abducens nerve paresis, ipsilateral facial (usually retroorbital) pain, and deafness

keySyndromes.name: Horner syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Miosis + ptosis (Muller muscle paresis) + anhidrosis of the forehead
keySyndromes.clue: Dilatation lag of the smaller pupil best separates it from physiologic anisocoria; anhidrosis is inconstant after postganglionic lesions. Anisocoria is greater in dim light with sympathetic lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: Horner syndrome comprises the triad of miosis, ptosis (due to paresis of Müller muscle), and anhidrosis of the forehead

boardTraps.text: A complete motor third nerve palsy with a normal pupil is rarely an aneurysm; the book still advises observation in the first week because some aneurysms develop delayed pupil involvement.
boardTraps.quote: The absence of an affected pupil in the setting of a complete motor oculomotor paresis almost always excludes a diagnosis of aneurysm.

boardTraps.text: Pupil findings are not absolute: in a population-based study pupil involvement did not exclude a microvascular palsy, and a spared pupil did not exclude a compressive one.
boardTraps.quote: pupil involvement did not exclude microvascular third nerve palsy and lack of pupil involvement did not rule out compressive third nerve palsy

boardTraps.text: An isolated medial rectus palsy is not a good nuclear localization, because medial rectus neurons are spread over three areas of the nucleus.
boardTraps.quote: it is unlikely that a medial rectus paralysis (unilateral or bilateral) would be the sole manifestation of a nuclear lesion

boardTraps.text: A superior or inferior division pattern is not proof of an orbital or sphenocavernous lesion; it can arise anywhere from the fascicle to the orbit.
boardTraps.quote: a divisional pattern may occur from damage anywhere along the course of the nerve

boardTraps.text: A trochlear palsy is not always contralateral to a midbrain lesion: interruption of the fascicle after its decussation gives an ipsilateral palsy.
boardTraps.quote: An ipsilateral trochlear palsy may result if the fascicle is interrupted after its decussation

boardTraps.text: Skew deviation versus fourth nerve palsy: torsion is opposite. In skew the hypertropic eye is intorted; in trochlear palsy it is extorted. Skew also usually comes with brainstem findings.
boardTraps.quote: the hypertropic eye is intorted with extorsion of the fellow eye (vs. the hypertropic eye being extorted with the fourth nerve palsy)

boardTraps.text: INO is not specific for etiology: bilateral INO is more common with MS, but both MS and infarction can cause unilateral or bilateral INO. Myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome can mimic it.
boardTraps.quote: the presence of a unilateral or bilateral INO cannot be used as a differential feature for etiologic diagnosis

boardTraps.text: Aberrant regeneration after a third nerve lesion points to compressive, traumatic, congenital or similar causes and is almost never seen after ischemic neuropathy.
boardTraps.quote: may be seen after oculomotor damage due to congenital causes, trauma, aneurysm, migraine, and syphilis but is almost never caused by ischemic neuropathy
